explanation: The sculptures combine Mediterranean techniques with Celtic motifs to create a "distinctly regional" style, so their aesthetic is unique, or singular. "Conventional" is tempting but means ordinary and standard, which contradicts the idea that the work is distinctive rather than derivative. "Fleeting" and "redundant" don't describe a lasting, original style.

The colon explains the blank: Kusunda has no demonstrable relationship to any other language family. A language like that is isolated. "Rudimentary" (basic, undeveloped) and "contentious" (disputed) don't match the claim of having no relatives.

The peptide kills bacteria, but its high toxicity to human kidney cells would likely rule out its use as a medicine, so "preclude" (prevent, make impossible) fits. "Anticipate" and "corroborate" don't express this negative effect, and "accentuate" would wrongly mean the toxicity highlights its usefulness.

The sentence contrasts a first impression of a "haphazard assembly" with what closer analysis shows: pavilions deliberately aligned on precise axes. The opposite of haphazard is an orderly, unified, or coherent layout. "Rudimentary" and "precarious" don't contrast with haphazard, and "superfluous" means unnecessary.

Kelley's records detailed exact temperatures, injury rates, and working hours, which shows they were thorough and complete: exhaustive. "Speculative" contradicts the precise data, and nothing in the text suggests the records were biased ("partisan") or outdated ("antiquated").

The underlined sentence shows Dorothea gradually ("day by day") seeing Casaubon's great work as a "labyrinth leading nowhere" instead of a monument, which stresses that the project lacks cohesion and progress. B is tempting because she sorts the notes, but the problem is the work itself, not her inability to organize. Nothing suggests deliberate concealment (C) or a contrast in reputation (D).

The following text is adapted from George Eliot’s 1871–1872 novel Middlemarch. Dorothea Brooke is contemplating the scholarly ambitions of her husband, Edward Casaubon.

Dorothea had believed that in marrying Mr. Casaubon she would be helping to construct a monumental edifice of knowledge that would illuminate ancient mythologies for all future ages. <u>Yet day by day, as she sorted through piles of disconnected notes and half-filled notebooks in the dim library, the great work began to look less like an enduring monument than an impenetrable labyrinth leading nowhere.</u> The massive synthesis remained unwritten, existing only in fragmentary outlines that seemed to multiply without advancing toward any definite conclusion.

explanation: The text describes a society that suppresses real feelings through strict rules, then shows Archer accepting those rules while sensing they may be a way "to avoid facing the reality of life." Its purpose is to explore his awareness of the tension between decorum and genuine experience. He doesn't try to reform the rules (A), leave society (C), or behave more openly than his peers (D).

The following text is adapted from Edith Wharton’s 1920 novel The Age of Innocence. Newland Archer reflects on the rigid social conventions governing elite New York society.

In the subtle and elaborate hierarchy of old New York, an unalterable code regulated every gesture, from the precise date for exchanging summer calls to the exact shade of gloves permissible at an evening opera. It was a world where real feelings were never mentioned, and where the direct expression of an opinion was regarded as almost indecent. Newland Archer had been bred in this atmosphere of delicate evasions; he accepted its decrees unquestioningly, yet he occasionally felt a faint stir of restlessness, a sudden fleeting suspicion that this meticulous preservation of form was merely a collective conspiracy to avoid facing the reality of life.

explanation: The underlined sentence reports what the researchers actually observed: grid-cell firing fields formed regular triangular lattices. The next sentence says this periodicity led them to conclude the brain builds an internal coordinate system, so the observation is the evidence for that conclusion. fix.passage: In an investigation of spatial cognition, neuroscientist Edvard Moser and colleagues examined how mammals maintain internal maps of physical environments. The team recorded the electrical activity of specialized neurons—known as grid cells—in the medial entorhinal cortex of rodents navigating open enclosures. <u>The firing fields of individual grid cells formed remarkably regular, periodic triangular lattices spanning the entire available area, closely matching mathematical models of hexagonal close-packing.</u> This spatial periodicity indicated to the researchers that the entorhinal cortex generates an intrinsic, metric coordinate system capable of computing distance and trajectory independently of external visual landmarks.

explanation: Gates argues that Fire!! rebelled against older leaders who wanted Black art to be respectable propaganda for white audiences. A contradicts this by crediting infrasound alone, and D overstates the finding by saying recognition fails at any distance.

The following text is adapted from Virginia Woolf’s 1927 novel To the Lighthouse. Lily Briscoe is attempting to capture a scene in a painting.

explanation: The underlined sentence describes Waddington's procedure (selective breeding over generations) and its result (flies with crossveinless wings even without heat). fix.passage: In evolutionary developmental biology, the concept of genetic assimilation describes a process by which an environmentally induced phenotype becomes fixed as an inherited trait through natural selection.
